title: Stand Still, Narrate and Stop: Small Classroom Changes with Big Impacts
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Effective classroom change doesn't require overhaul—it requires quiet intentionality about the 'how' before the 'what.' Five small, deliberate shifts transform classroom culture: standing still at the front during independent work, narrating do-nows with percentages, frontloading behavioral expectations, using mini-whiteboards for whole-class responses, and stopping lessons to reteach when understanding gaps emerge. Each shift is micro, but together they build a classroom where students think, persist, and take ownership. Standing still at the front while students work on a task is harder than circulating, but it signals that students must think for themselves and persevere through struggle. Teachers resist the urge to 'swoop in' and only move when students are working hard and independently. This trains students to expect thinking as non-negotiable and to see struggle as normal. Once students are engaged, teachers circulate, noting common errors and offering targeted support. Narrating the do-now review with percentages ('65% got question 2 right; 20% got question 6 correct') builds a culture of high visibility and normalizes mistake-making. It shows teachers value student work, builds collective accountability ('we are all learning together'), and creates psychological safety for students to acknowledge gaps without shame. Adding the collective pronoun 'we' throughout the day reinforces that classroom success is shared. Frontloading—placing behavioral expectations before the task itself—clarifies the hierarchy of importance and prevents ambiguity. Mini-whiteboards let teachers check understanding of the whole class at once instead of calling on one student and missing 29. Stopping to reteach when gaps appear closes misconceptions immediately rather than spending end-of-lesson time copying answers from the board.
points: Stand still at the front during independent work. Resist the urge to 'swoop in.' Only circulate once students are working hard and thinking. This signal trains students to expect thinking and perseverance as non-negotiable.
Narrate do-now results with percentages and collective language. This normalizes mistakes, builds psychological safety, and makes it clear that classroom success is shared, not individual.
Frontload behavioral expectations before the task. The first thing mentioned is the first thing students internalize as important.
Use mini-whiteboards for quick whole-class checks. Asking all 30 shows you who's got it, who doesn't, and where misconceptions are clustered.
Stop to reteach when you spot gaps during circulation. It saves time at the end and ensures students understand before moving on.
quotes: Learning is hard and in order for pupils to learn or understand, they must be thinking.
You may be helping, but you are actually making it so they do not think, they do not persevere and ultimately, do not learn.
This creates the culture in your classroom that the students must think for themselves and get themselves out of the struggle they find themselves in.
By placing the behavioural expectation at the start, I've established the how before the what.
If the whole class hasn't got a clue, reteach the concept and restart the timer.
Sometimes, the most profound classroom shifts aren't found in a new curriculum, a mandate from SLT, or fancy classroom tech.
But in the choice to stand silently at the front of your room.” Archived from Joel Kenyon @ Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
